title: Don Redman
summary: Redman gave him mouthpiece advice, and he recorded Redman's 'Cherry'.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Did you have any contact with McKinney's Cotton Pickers Group?
With Don Redman. No, that's, I was in school then.

Yeah, that's what I'm saying. I know you didn't have any, you know, actual physical, but, I mean, did you have any contact, when you were listening, or when you were feeding back, or any kind of influences
No. I didn't know too much of them. No. I knew about that band mostly after I got to New York.
After you got to New York. Right.

See? But, I met Don Redman. Well, Don Redman was in the Ubanqi, no. That was Connec's Inn, when I was in school. And, I used to listen to Don Redman come out of the Connec's Inn when I was in school. And when I got to New York, he was one of the first I met. And Don used to, you know, Don was a good trumpet player too. And he used to tell me, I used to wipe the wetness from my lips sometimes. He said oh, don't do it that way. He said wipe it from your mouthpiece. Let is stay there on your lip. You know? Now, that shows I got some more points from here, see? And he just explained it to me. And then when I did "Cherry" which is written by Don Redman, she thanked me all up and down Broadway there cause they had, Don had put that
tune away and the people weren't playing it anymore. And, he wrote that tune with McKinney's Cotton Pickers through those years.
